headline: 12 states settle. Paramount can buy Warner Bros.
summary: Twelve states sued in July to block Paramount's $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery. On Monday they settled. Paramount promised at least 30 films a year, more of them made in the US, a fund for laid-off workers, and a monitor on its news independence at CBS and CNN. Rob Bonta, who led the states, still says the two should not merge.

cover_question.q: So who owns Harry Potter now?

cover_answer: Paramount will, once the deal closes. Top Gun too.
table_question: Is a deal you don't believe in still worth taking?

5-7.script: The company that makes Top Gun is buying the company that makes Harry Potter. Twelve states said hold on, that's a lot for one company to own, and took it to court. On Monday they agreed: the deal can happen if Paramount makes at least 30 movies a year. It's like two big toy boxes tipped into one, with a grown-up counting what goes in.
5-7.why: Two toy boxes tipped into one is a picture. A merger is not. At this age one vivid detail stands in for the whole story, so the detail is the films they know, not the lawsuit.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script starts with two films they may know and a toy box, not with a merger. The grown-up counting what goes in is the monitor, the one part of the deal a child can picture. Expect "will Harry Potter go away?" No. The films stay. The question is who owns them.

8-12.script: Paramount is buying Warner Bros.: one owner for CBS, CNN, HBO Max and Harry Potter. Twelve states sued in July. On Monday they settled: 30 films a year, money for laid-off workers, a monitor to check Paramount keeps its word. A teacher letting two friends sit together, on conditions, and checking.
8-12.why: A chain that ends in a rule, and a teacher who checks. This age tests whether rules get enforced.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether rules get applied, and the settlement is a chain they can follow: a merger, a lawsuit, promises, a monitor. The teacher who sets conditions and checks back is the mechanism. Expect "why did the states give up?" Bonta still says they should not merge. He took promises he can enforce.

13-17.script: If you think two companies shouldn't merge, do you settle anyway? Rob Bonta did Monday: he still says the two shouldn't combine, but he traded a trial for 30 films a year and a monitor on CBS and CNN's news. Did he win, or fold?
13-17.why: Two true things: a win for workers, a loss for the case. A teenager can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things, and the script hands them the pair: Bonta says the companies should not merge, and Bonta signed the deal that lets them. The honest answer is that he bought promises he can enforce and gave up the trial. Expect "so did the states lose?" They stopped fighting. Whether that is losing is the argument.

5-7.a: No. The movies stay. A different company will own them, that's all.

8-12.q: So who owns Harry Potter now?
8-12.a: Paramount, with Top Gun too, once the deal closes in October.

8-12.q: Why did the states give up?
8-12.a: Bonta still says they shouldn't merge. He took promises he can enforce.

13-17.q: Why does it matter who owns CNN?
13-17.a: It puts a monitor on the independence of its news at CBS and CNN.

13-17.q: Will it cost more to watch stuff?
13-17.a: Alvaro Bedoya, ex-FTC commissioner, says your cable bill goes up.
